Issued at 132 PM EDT Sun Sep 13 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

In the closing days of summer 2026, there are no signs of autumn 
on the weather charts yet. Above-normal H5 heights continue to 
sprawl from the Desert Southwest to the western Atlantic. Jet 
stream energy is relegated to the northern tier of states this 
afternoon. At the surface, a dissipating cold front is settling 
over the southern Appalachians, leaving a high-pressure axis from
the Bahamas to the northern Gulf. A reservoir of above-normal 
moisture is still in place over Florida, characterized by PWATs 
over 2 inches.

South of a mid-level jet streak passing through the Great Lakes, 
global ensembles develop another impressive anticyclone over the 
Tennessee Valley by Tuesday and Wednesday. H5 heights may exceed 
600 dam near Great Smoky Mountains NP, which is nearly unheard of 
for mid-September. Its surface high-pressure reflection will tuck
beneath it, freshening easterly flow over Florida and the 
Carolinas. A sharp moisture gradient is likely to exist over 
Central Florida by Wednesday and Thursday as deep moisture is 
shunted toward the southern half of the state.

Cluster analysis of the 13/00Z ensemble suite suggests that pattern
retrogression will occur late in the week. As the mid-latitude
ridge nudges to the west, an upper-level trough is likely to be 
forced westward beneath it. This feature should reach Florida by 
late Thursday and Friday. By next weekend, this disturbance is 
forecast to push into the Gulf and begin to fill. Surface high 
pressure and onshore flow are both expected to weaken, and 
moisture values should return to normal over most of the 
peninsula.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

This Afternoon - Monday...

An increase in late-day showers and storms appears on track. 
Background winds are light WNW, which should limit Atlantic breeze
progression while a diffuse Gulf breeze propagates toward the 
eastern half of the state. Hi-res guidance focuses the highest 
coverage of storms between now and 9 PM along and especially west 
of I-95 (50-70%), with a potential collision of the sea breezes 
roughly near a line extending from Palm Coast to DeLand to Lake 
Okeechobee. Storms diminish by late evening and into the overnight.

On Monday, high pressure lifts northward a bit, allowing a better
push of the Atlantic breeze into the interior. Medium-high (50-60%)
coverage of late-day storms is again forecast, particularly from
Greater Orlando to along the Kissimmee Basin.

Over the next couple of days, Brief gusty winds to around 40-50 mph,
frequent lightning, and torrential rainfall will occur beneath the
strongest storms. REFS max-member 6-hour rainfall plots suggest
a reasonable worst case of 3-4" rainfall amounts, which may cause
localized flooding, particularly if it occurs over urban areas.

Hot and humid conditions continue to dominate. Highs reach the
low to mid 90s with heat indices as high as around 105 deg F.

Tuesday - Thursday...

Tuesday marks a transition in our weather pattern. As high pressure
strengthens to our north, onshore breezes will steadily increase off
the Atlantic. This will disrupt robust sea breeze convergence over
the peninsula for much of the work week. With deep moisture still
in place on Tuesday, another round of scattered storms is forecast
(50-70%) with the highest coverage over the interior by afternoon.

By Wednesday and Thursday, much drier air is expected to infiltrate
the northern third to half of the state, but ample moisture may
not be scoured out in the lowest 10 kft. Therefore, the setup
should transition into onshore-moving showers and a few storms. As
the upper-level trough approaches the state by late Thursday,
coastal moisture convergence may increase. While it's too early to
determine, a localized heavy rain threat may develop, especially
on the immediate Space and Treasure Coasts.

Breezy conditions develop beginning Tuesday afternoon, becoming
windy on Wednesday into at least early Thursday. Gusts may reach
up to around 30-35 mph on Wednesday. The fetch of onshore flow is
expected to cause rough surf and a high risk of rip currents at
Atlantic beaches beginning Tuesday night.

Highs should still reach the low 90s in most locations on
Tuesday. The increasing onshore breezes should then cause high
temps to trend into the mid-upper 80s on Wednesday and Thursday. 
Barrier island communities may struggle to fall below 80 degrees 
at night as the wind carries in warmth from the Atlantic shelf
waters and Gulf Stream.

Friday - Next Weekend...

The upper trough is forecast to be overhead on Friday before
pushing westward into the Gulf this weekend. As high pressure 
weakens, onshore flow and coastal convergence will follow suit.

scattered showers and storms through this period. High
